title: 2019–2026: The Post-QE Era
tagline: COVID pandemic · Inflation returns · The AI wave · Tariffs 2.0

sections.heading: Era Tone
body: This was the eight years in which the Fed's toolkit expanded without limit. In 2019 the US–China trade war and a yield-curve inversion forced the Fed to resume cutting (ending the tightening cycle that started in 2015); in 2020, COVID drove the Fed to zero within two weeks and pushed the balance sheet from $4.2 trillion to $9 trillion; in 2022, forty-year-high inflation triggered the most aggressive hiking cycle in Fed history (425bp in a year); cuts only returned in 2024. A complete 'crisis–rescue–tightening–easing' cycle compressed into six years — unprecedented.

AI was the structural through-line of the second half of the decade. ChatGPT arrived in November 2022; concentration in the 'Magnificent Seven' (Nvidia, Microsoft, Apple, Google, Amazon, Meta, Tesla) exploded in 2023, and by 2024 these seven companies were roughly 30% of S&P 500 market cap. Nvidia rose 170% in 2024 and its market cap briefly topped $4 trillion in 2025 — top-end concentration in US equities reached an all-time high.

Globalization went into its first systemic reverse. Trump's tariffs 1.0 in 2018 led to COVID supply-chain shocks in 2020, then the Russia-Ukraine war and Russia sanctions in 2022, then Trump's tariffs 2.0 in 2024–2025 (including steel/aluminum tariffs on allies, 145% tariffs on China, and 'secondary' rules targeting Chinese transshipment). 'Friend-shoring' and 'near-shoring' became the new supply-chain vocabulary.

The average federal deficit during these eight years was 7.5% of GDP — the highest in peacetime US history. Federal debt grew from $22 trillion in 2019 to $36 trillion in 2025, a 64% increase. Interest expense exceeded the defense budget for the first time in 2024. 'Fiscal-monetary deficit monetization,' once a theoretical idea, became operational policy — the most important macro setup for everything that follows.

items.body: The Fed cut three times between July and October 2019 (2.25–2.5% to 1.5–1.75%), ending the cycle that began in 2015. The 2-year/10-year curve inverted in August, signaling recession. The US–China trade war escalated, Hong Kong protests, Trump's impeachment, and the 737 MAX grounding all hit — yet the S&P 500 finished up 28.88%.

All-time high on February 19 → −34% by March 23 (the fastest bear market in history, 22 trading days) → all losses recovered by August 18 (the fastest new bull market in history). The Fed cut 150bp to zero between March 3 and March 15 and announced unlimited QE. The $2.2 trillion CARES Act passed. The BLM movement gathered force. Biden won on November 3. Pfizer/Moderna vaccines arrived in December.

Loose fiscal and monetary policy, supply-chain shocks, and rising oil pushed CPI from 1% to 7% over 2021. GameStop's retail short squeeze hit in January. Powell admitted in November 2021 that 'inflation is not transitory.' The Fed delivered 425bp across eight hikes in 2022, with a single 75bp move in June — the largest since 1994; June CPI hit 9.1%, the highest in forty years. The Russia-Ukraine war (February 24) and Russia sanctions sent energy prices higher.

Silicon Valley Bank's collapse in March 2023 triggered a regional bank crisis, but ChatGPT's one-year anniversary in November and Nvidia's GTC kicked off an AI capex boom. The Fed cut 100bp between July and December 2024. Trump won on November 5. The 'Liberation Day' tariffs in April 2025 imposed a 10% baseline on imports plus additional layers on China; DOGE (the Department of Government Efficiency) cut federal headcount. The lagged effects of the tariffs on inflation and supply chains continued playing out through 2026.

sections.heading: Economic Structure: AI Concentration and 'Friend-Shored' Manufacturing
body: Top-end concentration at all-time highs: in 2024 the Magnificent Seven accounted for ~30% of S&P 500 market cap and ~70% of the year's market gain. Market breadth (advance/decline line) diverged sharply from the index: through much of 2023–2024 the S&P 500 set new highs even as mid-caps went sideways. The 'top wins' indexing effect peaked alongside the AI wave.

Capex shifted to AI infrastructure: hyperscalers (Microsoft, Google, Meta, Amazon) collectively spent $300 billion on capex in 2024–2025, largely on AI compute (GPUs, data centers, power). Nvidia's data-center revenue grew from $15 billion in 2022 to $115 billion in 2024 — roughly 7x in two years from a single company.

Manufacturing reshoring remained more narrative than reality: the Inflation Reduction Act (IRA) of 2022 and the CHIPS Act subsidized semiconductor and clean-energy manufacturing. TSMC Arizona, Intel Ohio, and Samsung Texas received subsidies. But 2024 manufacturing employment was only 12.9 million, flat versus 2018. 'Friend-shoring' was more visible: from 2023 Mexico replaced China as the US's largest source of imports.

Fiscal monetization: 2020–2021 featured large direct stimulus payments ($1,200, $1,400, and $1,400) plus industrial-policy subsidies in the 2022 IRA. MMT moved from academic fringe to decision-making mainstream. Fed bond purchases financed more than 50% of the fiscal deficit at points in 2020–2021 — the line between fiscal and monetary policy effectively blurred.

sections.heading: Monetary Policy: From Toolkit to Toolshed
body: The March 2020 crisis response: the Fed cut 50bp on March 3, another 100bp to zero on March 15, and announced unlimited QE. Operation Twist was revived; crisis-era facilities such as the Primary Dealer Credit Facility (PDCF), the Commercial Paper Funding Facility (CPFF), and the Money Market Mutual Fund Liquidity Facility (MMLF) were resurrected. New facilities: Main Street Lending, the Municipal Liquidity Facility, and the PMCCF for primary corporate-bond purchases — the first time the Fed directly bought corporate-bond ETFs (including high-yield ETFs like HYG and JNK).

August 2021's Jackson Hole pivot: Powell acknowledged that inflation pressures were 'more persistent than expected.' He formally retired the 'transitory' framing in congressional testimony on November 30, 2021. The 2022 hiking pace broke records: starting with 25bp on March 16, 50bp on May 4, then four consecutive 75bp hikes on June 15, July 27, September 21, and November 2 — 425bp for the year.

March 2023 — the SVB crisis and the BTFP: Silicon Valley Bank failed on March 10, and the Fed launched the Bank Term Funding Program (BTFP) on March 12, allowing banks to pledge Treasuries at par (not market) value for funding. This 'par-value collateral' broke the traditional central-bank haircut principle and effectively delivered a hidden subsidy to mid-sized banks holding long-duration paper.
September 2024 cuts begin: fed funds went from 5.25–5.5% to 4.5–4.75% (November) and then 4.25–4.5% (December). In 2025 tariff-driven inflation pressure put the Fed into a 'hawkish pause.'
